summary: This informational document gives a framework for setting up and controlling MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineered label switched paths across multiple domains, where a domain is any set of network elements under common address management or path computation responsibility, such as an IGP area or an autonomous system.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes ways to establish traffic-engineered label-switched paths across multiple network domains. It separates the problem into how paths are computed, signaled, and supported by shared network information.

questions: what is inter-domain mpls traffic engineering
what is a path computation element
how are te lsps set up across multiple domains
subtitle: A framework for signaling and computing traffic-engineered MPLS paths across network domains.

tldr.problem: A traffic-engineered path may cross domains that do not share the same topology or path-computation responsibility.
tldr.mechanism: The framework separates LSP signaling, path computation, and distribution of reachability and traffic-engineering information. It describes nesting, contiguous paths, stitching, and several places where path computation can occur.
tldr.outcome: It names architectural options and trade-offs but does not define their protocols or select a universally best technique.

today: RFC 4726 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo describes a framework rather than a protocol.

sections.title: What Counts as a Domain
sections.content:
The framework applies to MPLS and GMPLS traffic-engineered Label Switched Paths (LSPs) that cross multiple domains. A domain is a collection of network elements with a common sphere of address management or path-computation responsibility; examples include IGP areas and Autonomous Systems.

The framework divides the work into discovering reachability and traffic-engineering information, computing an LSP path, and signaling that LSP. It is not a detailed protocol specification, and it excludes wholly or partly overlapping domains.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain is a group of network elements managed or planned together. A path crossing domains needs a way to compute the route and set it up across each boundary.

sections.title: Three LSP Signaling Options
sections.content:
The memo identifies three signaling approaches. With LSP nesting, one traffic-engineered LSP is carried inside a hierarchical LSP. With a contiguous LSP, a single LSP is established from ingress to egress in one signaling exchange and keeps the same Session/LSP ID along the path.

With LSP stitching, separately signaled LSP segments are joined in the data plane to form an end-to-end path. A single path may combine these approaches. The framework says the choice can depend on path computation, application, network topology, and switching capabilities; comparing applicability is left to other work.
sections.plainLanguage: A path can be carried inside another path, set up as one continuous LSP, or assembled from connected LSP segments. The framework allows combinations and does not choose one for every network.

sections.title: Where Path Computation Happens
sections.content:
An operator or offline tool can provide a path, which the ingress LSR encodes in an Explicit Route Object. Alternatively, the ingress can calculate the path if it has enough information. With partial visibility, it can provide explicit hops within its domain and looser information for later domains.

Domain-boundary LSRs can compute the next path segment, or a Path Computation Element can perform some or all of the computation. A PCE may return a complete path or only a partial path to help preserve topology confidentiality. Computation algorithms are outside this RFC's scope, and the document notes that summarized or abstracted information can prevent guaranteed optimal routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The route may be planned centrally, calculated at the entry point, filled in at domain boundaries, or computed by a PCE. How much topology each planner sees affects both path quality and confidentiality.

sections.title: Information Sharing and Operations
sections.content:
Path computation depends on reachability and traffic-engineering information, which is commonly distributed within a domain by IGP extensions. The framework discusses sharing information about links between domains, while warning that detailed information can create scaling and confidentiality concerns. Domain-boundary policies may filter or aggregate what is shared.

The memo also considers reoptimization, setup failure, repair, fast reroute, diverse paths, domain-specific constraints, operations and management, and non-packet technologies. Point-to-multipoint inter-domain requirements are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Planners need some information about how domains connect, but sharing too much can expose internal network details or burden the network. The framework also identifies issues to consider when paths fail or need improvement.

sections.title: Security Across Domains
sections.content:
Existing security procedures continue to apply within a domain. Inter-domain traffic engineering is more sensitive because control information crosses administrative boundaries, particularly between Autonomous Systems. The memo says a separate security analysis is needed before solution documents advance.

A domain may want to keep its topology and resource availability confidential. The domain distributing information is responsible for applying policy filters at its boundary. The memo also notes that coordinating authentication secrets across domains requires administrative coordination.
sections.plainLanguage: Domains may need to protect their internal maps and resource information. Security between domains depends on applying boundary policies and coordinating trust between administrators.
